title: N3
notes: Missing Magnification Clues (Signless Quantities)
"The size of the image is half the size of the object"
Meaning: the numerical value of magnification is |m| = 0.5.

How to decide the sign: if the mirror is convex, it must be a virtual image (Cartesian: m = +0.5, RIP: m = −0.5). If the mirror is concave, it must be a real image (Cartesian: m = −0.5, RIP: m = +0.5) because concave mirrors only produce diminished images when the object is beyond the center of curvature, which always results in a real image.
Hints about Magnification Sizes
"Magnified" / "Enlarged" → |m| > 1 (can only be produced by a Concave mirror).
"Diminished" / "Smaller" → |m| < 1 (can be produced by both, but if virtual, it must be Convex).
"Same size as the object" → |m| = 1 (object at Center of Curvature C of a Concave mirror; u = 2f).
Hints Embedded in Practical Applications

"A dentist holds a small mirror..." — Meaning: it is a concave mirror. Hidden Hint: dentists use these to see an enlarged, upright view of teeth, meaning the object (tooth) is placed between the focus and pole (u < f), creating a virtual, magnified image.

"Used as a solar furnace / solar cooker mirror" — Meaning: it is a concave mirror. Hidden Hint: sunlight comes from infinity (u = ∞); the mirror converges parallel rays to a point, so the heat/cooker must be placed exactly at the focus (v = f).
Multi-Step Physical Changes

"An object is moved closer to the mirror by 10 cm..." — Meaning: implies a two-state problem where u₂ = u₁ − 10. How to solve: find the initial focal length or object distance using the first scenario before mathematically altering the distance for the second scenario.

The Strict Constraints of Convex Mirrors
Convex mirrors have only one behavioral mode for any real object placed anywhere in front of them:
Condition: u can be anywhere from the pole to infinity.
Resulting Image Location: the image must always form behind the mirror, specifically between the Pole and the Focus (v < f).
Resulting Magnification: the image is always virtual, erect, and diminished (|m| < 1).
Rule: if you calculate an image for a convex mirror that is real, inverted, or magnified, your math is incorrect.
Absolute Mathematical Conditions (Sanity Checks)

The Real Object Condition: in real-world physics problems, the object is always real and placed in front of the mirror. Standard System: u must always be negative. RIP System: u must always be positive.

The Concave Mirror Virtual Exception: a concave mirror can only form a virtual image if the object is placed closer than the focal length (u < |f|). If your problem states the image is virtual and you're using a concave mirror, your calculated u must come out smaller than f.

The Focal Length Consistency: the focal length (f) is a physical property of the glass. It cannot change within the same problem unless the mirror is physically swapped. In two-step problems, calculate f in part 1, and plug that same value into part 2.
Zero and Infinite Edge Conditions
Condition for Zero Size: an image has zero size (m = 0) only when the object is infinitely far away (u = ∞).
Condition for Infinite Size: an image becomes infinitely large (m = ∞) only when the object is placed exactly on the focus (u = f).
Condition for Equal Distance: the image distance equals the object distance (|v| = |u|) only when the object is at the Center of Curvature (u = 2f).
Absolute Mathematical Formulas Summary

SystemMirror FormulaMagnification Formula
Standard Cartesian1/f = 1/v + 1/um = −v/u = hᵢ/hₒ
Real-is-Positive (RIP)1/f = 1/v + 1/um = v/u = −hᵢ/hₒ
Note: in the RIP system, m = v/u yields a positive sign for real/inverted images, which means a negative sign must be applied if relating it to the physical downward height ratio hᵢ/hₒ.
Alternative Variable Names
dₒ, p, or s → alternative symbols for Object Distance (u). dᵢ, q, or s' → alternative symbols for Image Distance (v). hₒ or h → Height of the Object. hᵢ or h' → Height of the Image.
Tricky Physical Conditions

"The mirror is partially covered / blacked out" — Meaning: if half of a concave mirror is covered with black paper, the full image is still formed. Hidden Hint: position, size, and nature of the image remain unchanged, but brightness/intensity decreases because less light is reflected.
"Object size is negligible / point object" — Meaning: the object is treated as a single point on the principal axis; only u and v matter, linear magnification heights (hᵢ) are ignored.

"A plane mirror is placed next to the spherical mirror..." — Meaning: a two-surface problem. The plane mirror forms a virtual image exactly as far behind it as the object is in front. Hidden Hint: questions will say "the two images coincide" — find where the plane mirror creates its image, then use that exact spatial location as the target value for the spherical mirror's image distance (v).
Common Exam Question Tricks
1. The "Double Magnification" Trick
The Trick: The question states: "A concave mirror forms an image 3 times the size of the object." It does not say if it is real or virtual.
The Trap: Students only calculate one position.

The Defeat: Concave mirrors can form both a real-magnified image (inverted) and a virtual-magnified image (erect). Solve twice — Case 1: take m as real (e.g. m = −3 in Cartesian). Case 2: take m as virtual (e.g. m = +3 in Cartesian).
2. The "Convex Mirror Magnification" Trap
The Trick: The question states: "A convex mirror forms an image magnified 2 times..."
The Trap: Students start calculating using m = 2.

The Defeat: This is a conceptual trick question. Convex mirrors can never magnify a real object; they only form smaller (diminished) images. The answer is immediately "Not physically possible" or "No such position exists."
3. The "Distance Between Object and Image" Trick
The Trick: The question says: "The distance between the object and its image is 10 cm."
The Trap: Students write down v − u = 10 or v = 10.

The Defeat: This means the absolute gap |v − u| = 10. Use the mirror type to figure out which is further away: for a convex mirror, the image is always closer to the mirror than the object, so (−u) − v = 10. For a concave mirror forming a real image, if the object is beyond C, the object is further away (u > v), so (−u) − (−v) = 10.
4. The "Liquid Immersion" Trick
The Trick: "A concave mirror of focal length 20 cm is completely immersed in a tank of water. Find its new focal length."
The Trap: Students use the refractive index of water (μ = 4/3) to change the focal length.
The Defeat: Mirrors do not change focal length in liquids. The focal length depends purely on the radius of curvature (f = R/2); this only applies to lenses. The focal length remains exactly 20 cm.
5. The "Object Shift" Trick
The Trick: An object is at 30 cm, then it is "shifted by 10 cm towards the mirror."
The Trap: Students miscalculate the new object distance.

The Defeat: Old distance: u₁ = −30 cm. New distance: shifted towards means it is closer, so u₂ = −(30−10) = −20 cm. Tip: always find the focal length (f) from the first scenario first, as it stays constant for the second scenario.
